statement: Use the substitution $x=\\sin^{2}\\theta$ to evaluate $I=\\int_{0}^{1}\\sqrt{x(1-x)}\,dx$, and show that $I=\\pi/8$.
solution:
With $x=\\sin^{2}\\theta$, $dx=2\\sin\\theta\\cos\\theta\,d\\theta$, and the limits become $\\theta=0$ to $\\pi/2$. Also $\\sqrt{x(1-x)}=\\sin\\theta\\cos\\theta$ (positive on this interval). Hence $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}(\\sin\\theta\\cos\\theta)(2\\sin\\theta\\cos\\theta)\,d\\theta=2\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\sin^{2}\\theta\\cos^{2}\\theta\,d\\theta=\\frac{1}{2}\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\sin^{2}2\\theta\,d\\theta=\\frac{1}{4}\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}(1-\\cos4\\theta)\,d\\theta=\\frac{1}{4}\left[\\theta-\\frac{1}{4}\\sin4\\theta\right]_{0}^{\\pi/2}=\\frac{1}{4}\\cdot\\frac{\\pi}{2}=\\frac{\\pi}{8}$.
